title: Interleaving practice
examples: Should I do all the algebra problems together or mix them up?
What is the difference between practicing one topic a lot and mixing topics?
How often should I mix up my practice questions?

explain.say: Today we are learning about interleaving practice for studying.
The first subtopic is using mixed problem sets for practice.
A concrete example is doing a quiz that mixes science and maths.
Another example is revising history and literature together.
The third subtopic is understanding why interleaving works so well.
In real life, interleaving is like studying for a big exam.

faq.q: Should I always mix topics when I study?
faq.a: It is helpful to mix topics often, but you should also spend time reviewing one topic deeply.
asks: Is it bad to study one thing all day?
Do I need to mix everything every time?

faq.q: What is the difference between interleaving and spacing?
faq.a: Spacing is about time gaps, while interleaving is about mixing subjects within one study session.

faq.q: If I only do mixed sets, will I forget the basics?
faq.a: You can lose the basics if you do nothing else, so always schedule time for focused review too.
asks: Do I need a review session?

faq.q: What is the best ratio for mixing topics?
faq.a: There is no set rule, but try to mix topics when you feel comfortable with the basics.
asks: How many topics should I mix?

faq.q: Can I use interleaving for subjects that are not academic?
faq.a: Yes, you can use it for skills like coding or learning languages by mixing different exercises.
asks: Can I use this for cooking skills?

facts: Interleaving means mixing different types of problems or topics during study.
It forces your brain to constantly switch between different sets of rules or knowledge.
This switching process strengthens your ability to select the correct strategy.
It is more effective for long-term retention than massed practice.

quiz.say: If you are studying physics and maths, which approach is best?
quiz.show: A) Do all the maths problems first, then all the physics problems.

options.show: D) Only study the topic I find easiest.
options.say: D) Only study the topic I find easiest.

options.show: B) Mix a maths problem with a physics problem, then repeat.
options.say: B) Mix a maths problem with a physics problem, then repeat.

options.show: A) Do all the maths problems first, then all the physics problems.
options.say: A) Do all the maths problems first, then all the physics problems.

options.show: C) Study maths for two hours and physics for two hours.
options.say: C) Study maths for two hours and physics for two hours.

quiz.why: Mixing topics forces your brain to retrieve different rules, which strengthens memory.

wrong.0: You must challenge yourself to build knowledge in harder areas too.
wrong.2: This is called 'blocking' and it makes you good at one thing but bad at switching.
wrong.3: This is too much time on one topic and doesn't build switching skills.

quiz.say: What is the main benefit of mixing topics when studying?

options.show: The ability to switch between different concepts.
options.say: The ability to switch between different concepts.

options.show: Reducing the total amount of study time.
options.say: Reducing the total amount of study time.

quiz.why: The act of switching between different rules or ideas is the skill that gets stronger.

wrong.0: Good study skills require tackling the difficult parts as well.
wrong.2: While you learn facts, the main benefit is the process of recalling them.
wrong.3: Interleaving might take slightly longer initially, but it saves time later.

quiz.why: Interleaving specifically means mixing different, related topics together for practice.

wrong.0: Concept mapping is about showing relationships between ideas, not the practice method itself.
wrong.2: Spaced repetition refers to reviewing material over increasing time gaps, not mixing topics.
wrong.3: Massed practice means studying one topic intensely for a very long time.
